title: Polynomial-time DNF learning from uniform random examples
aliases: Efficient learning of disjunctive normal forms
decision_reason: Explicit uniform examples-only question, independently authored status corroboration including 2026 sources, current full relevant scope comparisons, duplicate screening and separated A38 self-pass completed. One underlying DNF family; no active ID until batch integration.

problem_fingerprint.model_or_objects: Unknown Boolean f represented by an OR of at most s conjunctions of literals x_j or NOT x_j; the representation is not given to the learner.
problem_fingerprint.dimension: Arbitrary positive integers n and s.
problem_fingerprint.domain: Input cube {0,1}^n with the uniform probability law.
problem_fingerprint.regularity_and_data_class: All Boolean functions with an s-term DNF representation, arbitrary widths, signs, overlap and relevant variables; noiseless realizable labels.
problem_fingerprint.parameter_range: Every n,s>=1 and accuracy/confidence parameters epsilon,delta in (0,1/2). A bound s is supplied, not the target formula.
problem_fingerprint.quantifiers: There exist one classical randomized learner and one polynomial p that work for every n,s,epsilon,delta and every such unknown f.
problem_fingerprint.normalization: Uniform independent bits; s counts terms, each of length at most n, so literal-size and term-size polynomial bounds agree.
problem_fingerprint.observable_or_norm: Uniform classification error Pr_X[h(X)!=f(X)] at most epsilon, with probability at least 1-delta over samples and internal randomness.
problem_fingerprint.limit_regime_and_order: One polynomial bounds all parameters jointly; no fixed-s exponent or input-dependent advice.
problem_fingerprint.requested_conclusion: Existence or nonexistence of an examples-only efficient PAC learner, with improper efficiently evaluatable Boolean hypotheses allowed.
problem_fingerprint.computational_model_and_dependencies: Classical randomized computation; only independent labeled examples (X,f(X)), X uniform. Training time, samples, output description and hypothesis evaluation are bounded by p(n,s,1/epsilon,log(1/delta)). All preprocessing is charged. No membership, similarity, random-walk or quantum example oracle.

statement_source_and_scope_match: Yang–Blum–Carbonell, author manuscript §§1.1–1.2, explicitly identifies the uniform random-examples-only gap. Feldman arXiv:1203.0594 §2 p.5 defines iid EX access and permits polynomial dependence on the number s of terms; Alman–Nadimpalli–Patel–Servedio §1.1 explicitly distinguishes arbitrary efficiently evaluatable hypotheses from proper DNF hypotheses and explains confidence amplification. These are used together to state the standard all-parameter problem, not to impose proper learning.

proposed_statement_text:
For positive integers $n,s$, let $\mathcal D_{n,s}$ be the Boolean functions on $\{0,1\}^n$ representable as a disjunction of at most $s$ terms. Each term is a conjunction of literals, and a literal is either a coordinate $x_j$ or its negation $1-x_j$. Term lengths, overlaps and signs are unrestricted.

Does there exist a classical randomized algorithm $A$ and a polynomial $p$ with the following property? For every $n,s$, every unknown $f\in\mathcal D_{n,s}$, and every $\varepsilon,\delta\in(0,1/2)$, the algorithm is given $n,s,\varepsilon,\delta$ and access only to independent labeled examples
$$
(X,f(X)),\qquad X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\{0,1\}^n).
$$
Within time at most
$$
p\!\left(n,s,\varepsilon^{-1},\log(1/\delta)\right),
$$
it outputs a description of a Boolean function $h:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ satisfying
$$
\Pr_{\text{training examples and algorithm}}\!
\left[
\Pr_{X\sim\operatorname{Unif}(\{0,1\}^n)}
\{h(X)\ne f(X)\}\le\varepsilon
\right]\ge1-\delta?
$$

The inner probability uses a fresh input. Reading examples and all preprocessing count toward the runtime; evaluating the resulting hypothesis on any input must also take polynomial time in the same parameters. The algorithm receives a size bound, not a formula for $f$. It may output a hypothesis outside the DNF class. Neither chosen label queries nor quantum examples are available. This is the noiseless, examples-only uniform-distribution PAC-learning question. [1–3]
applied_significance: DNFs encode alternative combinations of binary features. The question separates availability of a compact rule model and polynomial sample information from efficient prediction using passive observations. Uniform input is an idealized benchmark; improper learning need not identify an interpretable rule formula.
open_status_evidence_summary: YBC13 explicitly identifies this exact question; KRS19 and independently authored C26 retain the access distinction. ANPS25 and CGKSV26 discuss the continuing quasipolynomial examples-only baseline. Checked plausible positive and negative results change the oracle, input law, target family, success quantifier or runtime.
independent_status_corroboration: YBC13, KRS19 and C26 have disjoint author sets. ANPS25, HK26 and CGKSV26 give further independently authored current scope evidence. Versions of a paper are one source, ANPS25B shares all ANPS25 authors, and AFK13 overlaps F13/KRS19.
strongest_known_partial_results_and_gap: The general uniform examples-only bound recalled in ANPS25 is n^{O(log(s/epsilon))} at constant confidence, with standard amplification. Polynomial algorithms are known under stronger oracle access. No claim of optimality is made for every parameter regime.

normalization_review: Replacing {-1,1} bits by {0,1} preserves uniform input and DNF literal representations.
Number of literals is at most ns, so conventional term/literal size choices give polynomially equivalent complexity requirements.
Known size bound s need not reveal the representation.

Confidence amplification: repeat a constant-success learner O(log(1/delta)) times with smaller target error, evaluate candidates on fresh labeled examples, and select by empirical error; all costs remain polynomial. This is consistent with ANPS25 footnote 1.

Elementary sample-bound inference: at most (3^n+1)^s padded formulas imply log class size O(ns); exhaustive consistent search needs O((ns+log(1/delta))/epsilon) iid examples. This is not an efficient search algorithm.
